context.description: Adelaide is the capital of South Australia, set on a plain between the Adelaide Hills and Gulf St Vincent. Colonel William Light laid it out as a grid of wide streets surrounded by parklands, and the plan largely survives. North Terrace holds the state museum, art gallery and botanic garden, while the Central Market and Rundle Mall sit a few blocks south. Famous wine regions, including the Barossa, McLaren Vale and the Adelaide Hills, border the city.

context.description: The Adelaide Hills are the wooded ranges east of Adelaide, reached in about half an hour. Hahndorf, founded by German settlers, anchors the region with its main street of galleries and bakeries. Around it are cool-climate vineyards, farms and national park bushland with lookouts over the city and plains. Mount Lofty, at 710 m, is the high point of the ranges.

context.description: The Barossa Valley is a wine region about an hour's drive north of Adelaide, with Tanunda, Nuriootpa and Angaston as its main towns. German settlers shaped its villages, bakeries and restaurants, and large cellar doors such as Penfolds and Seppeltsfield stand alongside small family wineries. Lookouts on the ranges above the valley floor give views across the vineyards, and the old copper town of Kapunda marks its western edge.

context.description: The Clare Valley is a wine region in South Australia's Mid North, about two hours' drive north of Adelaide. The Riesling Trail follows a former railway line past cellar doors between Auburn and Barinia, and Sevenhill Cellars, founded by Jesuits, is the valley's first winery. Mintaro's slate-and-stone streets and Martindale Hall recall the pastoral wealth of the 1800s, while Spring Gully and Neagles Rock add waterfall and lookout walks.
